items.title: As many of you know, I find corporate earnings to be a valuable complement to macroeconomic data when gauging economic trends. Not so this morning as two important US retailers offered contrasting signals on where things are headed: Lowe’s trimmed its 2026 outlook, pointing to high interest rates and a challenging macro environment, while Target raised its guidance on the back of resilient consumer spending. The focus now shifts to Walmart’s earnings. #economy #markets @Lowes @Target @Walmart

items.title: Now YCC is far from a free lunch. While it can help bring down longer-end yields in the immediate/short term, thus helping mortgage and other borrowing costs, it risks collateral damage and unintended consequences. Morever, the effects of this financial engineering are short dated unless followed by fundamental policy adjustments. #economy #yields #bonds #markets

items.content:
This Bloomberg chart illustrates the previous comment that higher government bond yields are a global phenomenon.
What makes this cycle different from past ones includes:
G7 Vulnerability: The debt cycle spotlight is as much on G7 economies (France, Japan, and the UK in particular) as on developing countries.
Less Elastic Drivers: The primary catalysts driving yields higher—massive corporate and government supply and, to a lesser extent, oil prices—are less responsive to central bank monetary policy.
Lagged Economic Responses: The repricing out of tech and government bond issuance will lag the damage that higher yields could inflict on traditionally rate-sensitive sectors, including housing, autos, and highly leveraged finance.
 #economy   #markets   #debt   #yields 
— Mohamed A. El-Erian (@elerianm) Aug 18, 2026

items.title: Olivier’s excellent post below builds on his widely discussed framework of twin debt equilibria dynamics for France and other highly indebted entities. It illustrates how quickly self-reinforcing dynamics can flip: A benign regime of low risk premia and sustainable debt service can rapidly deteriorate following an investor sentiment shift, exogenous shock, etc. This type of regime fragility has been familiar to emerging economies. Increasingly, it is a risk dynamic that is relevant to some advanced economies. #economy #markets #debt @ojblanchard1
items.content:
Olivier’s excellent post below builds on his widely discussed framework of twin debt equilibria dynamics for France and other highly indebted entities.
It illustrates how quickly self-reinforcing dynamics can flip:
A benign regime of low risk premia and sustainable debt service can rapidly deteriorate following an investor sentiment shift, exogenous shock, etc.
This type of regime fragility has been familiar to emerging economies. Increasingly, it is a risk dynamic that is relevant to some advanced economies.
 #economy   #markets   #debt   @ojblanchard1 Olivier Blanchard (@ojblanchard1)Useful to summarize the discussion  about debt and spreads in a graph (based on work with  @pmbruera and  @Gonhuertas . Working paper out soon).

The blue line shows the “good equilibrium” if investors are rationally optimistic. At very low debt, no risk of default, no spread, then a slow increase, and eventually a sudden  jump and default. So, if things get worse (high continuing deficits, increasing debt ratio), reasons to worry.

But, even if things do not get worse, and investors turn (rationally) pessimistic, they require a larger spread, the interest rate jumps and default happens faster. 

I think France is roughly at point A: small spread, but reasons to worry. Deficit is too large, so France keeps moving to the right. And, even if not, equilibrium could jump to point B, with a higher spread.—  https://x.com/ojblanchard1/status/2089626328253214969 
— Mohamed A. El-Erian (@elerianm) Aug 18, 2026

items.title: Staying on the topic of interest rates, this from Bloomberg on market expectations for central bank policies: "Traders see borrowing costs rising faster in Japan, Canada, the euro zone and the UK than in the US over the next year. Of the 32 swap markets tracked by Bloomberg, two-thirds are priced for rate hikes, with South Korea leading the pack at more than 100 basis points. It marks a shift from the Fed-dominated rate cycle of recent years." More to follow on the "why" and the "so what." #economy #markets #centralbanks

items.title: While on economic activity in Asia, China’s July industrial production growth slowed to 4.5%, missing the consensus forecast. Combined with lower-than-expected retail sales, today’s IP numbers confirm the narrative of a dual-track Chinese economy that spans both supply and demand factors: One consists of booming sectors fueled by tech and strong exports. The other is dominated by struggling sectors comprising more traditional production and weak domestic consumption. #economy #markets #China #growth #Asia

items.title: Japan’s Q2 GDP Growth Misses Expectations At an annualized rate of 1.1%, Japan's second-quarter GDP growth fell short of both the prior quarter’s 2.1% and the 2.0% consensus forecast. The policy implications of this miss are more consequential given the domestic measures required to support the yen, particularly as the impact of the joint currency intervention continues to erode (please see weekly note). Meanwhile, market pressure remains evident, with 10-year Japanese government bond yields rising to 2.92%, the highest level since 1996. (Reuters headline below.) #economy #Japan #growth #yen #currency
items.content:
